data.name: Dronraj
data.gender_notes: Dronraj is used as a male name in Hindu naming traditions.
data.long_meaning: Dronraj is the name of the legendary sage and charioteer of Arjuna in Hindu mythology. He is considered a guru, a guide, and a master of weapons. He imparted knowledge to Arjuna through the Bhagavad Gita, and his teachings are an essential part of Hindu spirituality. The name Dronraj carries the meaning “Lord of the chariot” and is chosen by families in Hindu traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Sanskrit tradition and is also used in Hindi, Sanskrit, Marathi. Parents who choose Dronraj usually hope their child will grow to embody lord of the chariot and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.etymology: Dronraj belongs to the Sanskrit linguistic tradition and is used in Hindu naming. Its recorded meaning is “Lord of the chariot.”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Dronraj total 8, giving a life-path number of 8. Number 8 is linked with Saturn and with the qualities of ambition, resilience and material success.

data.cultural_impact: Dronraj is a revered figure in Indian culture, not just due to his role as Duryodhana's charioteer, but primarily because he was the esteemed teacher of Arjuna, the greatest warrior in Hindu mythology. The teachings he imparted in the form of the Bhagavad Gita underscore essential moral and philosophical aspects of Indian life. Moreover, the spellbinding narrative of the Mahabharata, the great Indian epic, highlights the importance of guru-shishya (teacher-student) relationships, which have a profound influence on Indian society. In everyday life, the respect for the role of teachers in guiding and shaping the lives of their students remains deeply ingrained in the Indian mindset. Thus, the name Dronraj often evokes reverence and reminds us of the significance of learning and wisdom.
data.spiritual_significance: Dronraj, as the name implies, symbolizes knowledge, wisdom, and kindness. In Hinduism, he is revered as an embodiment of the divine teacher who imparts life-altering knowledge. The Bhagavad Gita, which he shared with Arjuna, forms the philosophical cornerstone of Hindu spirituality, emphasizing the path of devotion, selfless work, and compassionate action as means to attain enlightenment and liberation from the cycle of birth and rebirth. With Lord Krishna as the speaker and Dronraj as the messenger, the Bhagavad Gita continues to inspire millions worldwide and is regarded as one of the most significant spiritual texts in the world. In essence, the name Dronraj signifies the pursuit of knowledge, wisdom, and spiritual growth that can lead us towards greater self-awareness and inner fulfillment.
data.spiritual_symbolism: Dronraj: The radiant sage Drona, symbolizing wisdom and knowledge, illuminating the path to dharma and righteousness. His divine aspect, Raj, represents the king of one's inner self, guiding towards self-rule and enlightenment.

vedic_reference.note: Dronraj is the name of the great sage and teacher, Dronacharya, who was the preceptor of the Kuru and Pandava princes in the Mahabharata epic.

historical_references.reference: Drona was a great teacher of warriors in Mahabharata. He was the preceptor of the Kuru and Pandava princes. After the Kurukshetra war, Drona's son Ashwatthama attacked the Pandava camp, as per the promise made to Duryodhana before the war, to avenge the death of Bhishma and Duryodhana. This event is known as the Ashwatthama's night attack or the Smashana Parva.
historical_references.context: Mahabharata war, Indian mythology and Hinduism

historical_references.reference: Drona, also known as Dronacharya, was a great warrior, teacher, and sage in ancient India. He was the guru of both the Pandavas (the good side) and the Kauravas (the evil side) in the Mahabharata war. Drona was considered invincible in battle as long as his flag, his standard, was unfurled. He is also known for his curse by Draupadi, which led to his eventual demise in the war.
historical_references.context: Mahabharata war, Indian mythology and Hinduism
